news.title: Donald Trump Says He Would 'Love' to Have John Fetterman as a Republican
news.text: President Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love" to see Democratic Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania become a Republican, renewing speculation about the senator's future after months of high-profile breaks with his party. "I'd love to see him as a Republican," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews as he returned from a rally in Tennessee. "If you look at the polls, he does better as a Republican than he does as a Democrat." Trump added that Fetterman is a "very solid person" and "has great common sense." The president also said that Fetterman has "magnificent parents," and that he "got to speak to his parents about something." The comments were among Trump's clearest public efforts yet to encourage Fetterman to join the GOP at a time when control of the Senate remains in play ahead of next month's midterm elections. Newsweek has reached out to Fetterman's office for comment. Fetterman Has Repeatedly Rejected a Party Switch Despite growing speculation, Fetterman has consistently said he does not intend to become a Republican. Writing in The Washington Post in May, Fetterman described himself as a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats." Still, the Pennsylvania senator has frequently frustrated fellow Democrats by breaking with the party on several issues, including immigration and support for Israel. Concerns among Democrats intensified last month when Fetterman recorded a video for a Republican midterm convention praising fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick, a Republican. In the video, Fetterman criticized what he described as political extremism. "I'm always going to stand with America," Fetterman said. "I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life." Trump's latest comments come as Democrats try to regain control of the Senate. Democrats need to gain four seats to reclaim the majority, though the electoral map remains challenging. The president also suggested Fetterman could face difficulties winning another Democratic Senate nomination if his clashes with the party continue. What Polling Says About John Fetterman In his remarks at Joint Base Andrews, Trump said "it's going to be hard" for Fetterman to win the 2028 Democratic primary as a Democrat. While a party switch has generated significant media attention, polling has painted a more complicated picture of Fetterman's political standing. An Inquirer/New York Times/Siena College poll published in August found Fetterman had become more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans than fellow Republican Senator Dave McCormick. The survey found 73 percent of registered Republican voters viewed Fetterman favorably, compared with 63 percent who viewed McCormick favorably. At the same time, support for Fetterman among Democrats had fallen sharply. Just 22 percent of Democratic voters viewed him favorably, compared with 74 percent two years earlier, according to the survey. Other polling has pointed in a different direction. A February 2026 Quinnipiac University poll found that 72 percent of Pennsylvania Democrats approved of Fetterman's job performance, compared with 34 percent of Republicans, while independents were closely divided. Together, the surveys suggest Fetterman remains a politically unusual figure whose support varies significantly depending on the electorate and the questions being asked. Newsweek previously reported that his support for Israel, willingness to work with Republicans, and criticism of fellow Democrats had won praise from many conservative voters while straining relationships within his own party. That dynamic creates a political dilemma. A move to the Republican Party could potentially improve Fetterman's standing with GOP voters but risk alienating the Democratic coalition that helped elect him in 2022. Despite recurring speculation about a party switch, Fetterman has repeatedly rejected the idea. In May, he wrote that he would be a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats." Party Switches Can Reshape Senate Control The Senate has seen several high-profile party switches over the years, some of which altered the balance of power in Washington. The last senator whose switch directly changed control of the chamber was Jim Jeffords of Vermont. He left the Republican Party in 2001 and caucused with Democrats, helping give them a narrow majority, according to the Associated Press. Former Pennsylvania Senator Arlen Specter also made headlines in 2009 when he left the GOP and joined Democrats, a move that helped strengthen the party's Senate majority during President Barack Obama's first year in office. For now, however, Fetterman continues to identify as a Democrat and has repeatedly rejected suggestions that he plans to leave the party, even as polls show him attracting unusually strong support from Republican voters. news.title: WHO unsure what caused pneumonia that killed plague-lab worker in Russia
news.text:
GENEVA (Reuters) : The World Health Organization said on Saturday that it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a Russian lab worker at an anti-plague research center in Siberia this month, and that no case of plague had been registered.

The WHO said the Russian state regulator reported that tests of the lab worker and those who came in contact with her were negative ⁠for the high-threat ⁠pathogens tested, that her contacts still showed no symptoms, and that no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been identified.

“Based on the information provided … (the) WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key ⁠uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker,” it said in a statement.

The lab worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on October 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears on social media.

Global health officials have been extra alert to fatal pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with ⁠a ⁠cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China. The cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined.

Russian authorities have said the lab worker was appropriately vaccinated and that they found no microorganisms linked to her work in her body.

On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all the worker’s contacts. It says it had provided full information to the WHO according to established procedures.

news.title: Samosa Caucus set to shrink as two Indian Americans exit
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 11 (IANS) The number of Indian Americans in the US House of Representatives is set to fall from six to four after the November 3 midterm elections unless Democrats Amish Shah in Arizona or Pia Dandiya in Florida win their closely fought races, as Congressmen Raja Krishnamoorthi and Shri Thanedar prepare to leave the chamber. All six Indian-American members of the current House, informally known as the "Samosa Caucus", are Democrats: Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Krishnamoorthi, Thanedar and Suhas Subramanyam. Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois's 8th Congressional District, gave up his seat to run for the Senate. He lost the March 17 Democratic primary to Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton, who won 40.39 per cent of the vote to his 32.71 per cent. "Obviously, this is not the result we sought… But unlike Donald Trump, I'm not going to question the outcome. I'm proud of the race we ran," Krishnamoorthi said in his concession. Thanedar lost the August 4 Democratic primary in Michigan's 13th Congressional District to state Representative Donavan McKinney, 48.1 per cent to 51.9 per cent. Justice Democrats spent nearly $1 million backing McKinney, who was also endorsed by Senator Bernie Sanders. "I want to congratulate Representative Donavan McKinney on a hard fought race… It was the honor of my life to represent the 13th District in the United States Congress," Thanedar said in a Facebook statement on August 5. The other four Indian-American incumbents are on the ballot in seats rated Solid or Safe Democratic by the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball. They are Bera in California's 3rd District, Khanna in California's 17th, Jayapal in Washington's 7th and Subramanyam in Virginia's 10th. In two of those races the community wins either way. Khanna faces Indian-American Republican Ritesh Tandon, while Jayapal faces Indian-American Republican Nirav Sheth. That leaves two possible pickups. In Arizona's 1st Congressional District, Shah, an emergency room physician, faces Trump-backed Republican Jay Feely. The Cook Political Report moved the race from Toss-up to Lean Democratic on September 25, while Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball rate it a Toss-up. The only public October poll, by FirstStrategic, has Shah at 44 per cent and Feely at 42 per cent, within the survey's margin of error of 5.4 points. Shah narrowly lost the seat to Republican David Schweikert in 2024. "Now, it's my job to earn the support of every voter in this district—including Democrats who voted for another candidate, Independents frustrated with our political system, and Republicans disappointed with the state of the country," Shah said after winning the Democratic primary in July. In Florida's redrawn 22nd Congressional District, an open seat, Dandiya faces Republican Casey Askar. Cook rates the race a Toss-up, Inside Elections rates it Tilt Republican and Sabato's Crystal Ball has it as Lean Republican. Trump won the new seat 55-44 in 2024. Polling is sparse. A survey by Impact Research for House Majority PAC, a Democratic sponsor, put Dandiya at 46 per cent and Askar at 44 per cent, while an August poll by Tavern Research showed the two tied. Dandiya, a former teacher and principal born in Palm Beach County to parents who immigrated from India, would be Florida's first South Asian member of Congress. "I am so thrilled and honoured to be your Democratic nominee for US Congress here in my home state of Florida," she said in her primary victory speech in August. The caucus cannot grow beyond six in January, as no other Indian American is a competitive House nominee. Republicans Tandon, Sheth and Mahesh Ganorkar, who faces Democrat Valerie Foushee in North Carolina's 4th District, are all running in Solid Democratic seats. The departures come in a difficult cycle for incumbents. Twelve sitting House members lost primaries this year, seven of them Democrats. Before 2012, only two Indian Americans had served in Congress: Democrat Dalip Singh Saund of California, from 1957 to 1963, and Republican Bobby Jindal of Louisiana, from 2005 to 2008. Bera's election in 2012 began a steady rise. Khanna, Jayapal and Krishnamoorthi arrived in 2017, Thanedar in 2023 and Subramanyam in 2025. Indian Americans number about 5.5 million, roughly 1.6 per cent of the US population. In an AAPI Vote/AAPI Data survey this summer, Indian-American voters favoured Democratic House candidates by 66 per cent to 18 per cent.

news.title: PM Shehbaz condemns Houthi attack on Saudi airport that killed 12, wounded over 300
news.text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday condemned a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, in which at least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured.

Reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, the prime minister maintained that targeting civilian and critical infrastructure was “completely unacceptable and [constitutes] a serious threat to regional peace and stability.

He stressed that such acts of violence, which flagrantly violate international law, must cease immediately.

Expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia, Shehbaz reiterated Pakistan’s unwavering commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security, citing the joint defence agreement and the longstanding bonds of brotherhood between the two countries.

Houthis hit Riyadh airport again

The development comes after Houthis targeted, for the third time this week, Riyadh’s international airport, leaving at least 12 ​people dead and more than 300 wounded, Saudi authorities said.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strike.

The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, they said 309 were wounded.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.

Saturday’s attack occurred without warning, with no alert issued by ​Saudi Arabia’s threat warning system. This week’s two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi ​commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

This week’s deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s self-defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign ⁠against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the group.

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets ​in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women and children.

Also read: Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport killed three as war escalates

Reuters could not independently verify those claims.

All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at ​the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had “shut down Riyadh international airport”. The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive ​against the group on Monday.

US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

“We may. We’re ​going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.

EYEWITNESS SAW WOUNDED ON THE GROUND

One eyewitness at the ‌airport on ⁠Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

The US embassy in Riyadh said it was “aware of attacks” and “strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas.”

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the ​head of an Arab coalition to try to ​force the Houthis out of the ⁠Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.

The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the ​conflict.

Also read: Houthis say they hit Saudi sites with missiles, drones

That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb ​from Saudi-backed government forces.

The ⁠Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country’s third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

RIYADH DUE TO HOLD MAJOR SUMMITS

Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Houthi ⁠attacks on Thursday ​and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services ​to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organizers of those conferences said on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, and they sought to reassure attendees of their security.

news.title: Trust in science falls as Covid-era confidence fades, finds global survey
news.text: By Jason Gale The Covid-era surge in public trust in science has largely faded, with the steepest drop among people struggling financially, according to one of the largest global surveys of attitudes toward science. Across countries surveyed before, during and after the pandemic, 72% of people expressed at least some trust in science in 2025, down from 80% in 2020 and 77% in 2018. Strong trust in scientists also dropped below its pre-pandemic level, according to the Wellcome Global Monitor, which surveyed more than 140,000 adults worldwide. The retreat has potentially far-reaching consequences for public health as vaccination rates decline and preventable diseases resurge. The US is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in three decades, with almost 3,900 cases this year, while childhood vaccination rates have fallen below levels needed to prevent outbreaks in many communities. The findings come as misinformation and conspiracy theories complicate responses to health threats, and scientific institutions in some countries face growing political and funding pressures. The survey doesn’t establish what caused the decline, though the politicization of science during the pandemic probably contributed, said John-Arne Røttingen, chief executive officer of Wellcome, a London-based health research foundation. Vaccines, masks and public-health measures became politically contested, he said. “Politics has made some of science more political and that has led to the polarization and maybe a lack of trust,” Røttingen said in an interview from Berlin. The decline was particularly pronounced among people experiencing financial hardship. In 2025, 39% of those who said they were living comfortably reported a lot of trust in science, compared with 20% among those who find it difficult to get by. That divide has widened since the pandemic. Strong trust fell 16 percentage points among those struggling financially between 2020 and 2025, compared with 10 points among those living comfortably. Countries with greater economic inequality also tended to have lower trust in science, as did places where people had less confidence in public institutions or perceived greater corruption. People struggling financially may see science as part of a broader system that isn’t working for them, Røttingen said. “Science is seen as one of those institutions that are not delivering,” he said. Scientists also need to do a better job of reaching such communities, he said. “We haven’t been good enough at explaining and engaging with those groups and those communities on how science is benefiting them.” Experiences with healthcare were also closely associated with trust. While 26% globally said they had a lot of trust in science, that rose to 43% among people with a lot of confidence in their country’s hospitals and health clinics. The survey, produced by Wellcome with Gallup and Ipsos, points to a connection between trust and vaccinations. When respondents were asked what they do when a doctor or nurse recommends a vaccine, 34% said they wanted it immediately, 48% preferred to think about it and 15% said they didn’t get vaccines at all. Those who wanted a recommended vaccine immediately were twice as likely to express a lot of trust in science as those who didn’t vaccinate — 36% versus 18% — though Wellcome cautioned that other factors also shape vaccine decisions. Falling vaccination coverage shows how mistrust can have consequences beyond the individual because vaccines also protect people in the wider community who can’t be vaccinated or don’t mount a strong immune response, Røttingen said. “I am worried” about rising measles cases in the US and Europe, he said. Public willingness to use new vaccines and other technologies will also be crucial in future health emergencies, he said. “The power of science can only be fully realized if people trust the science and trust the technologies coming from science.” Political DividePolitics also appears to shape Americans’ views of science. The share saying science benefits most people rose to 57% in 2025 from 48% in 2018, bucking a global decline. Yet views were sharply divided along political lines. Among Americans who disapproved of their country’s leader, 74% said science benefited people like them “a lot,” compared with 44% among those who approved. The survey was conducted after Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election but while Joe Biden was still president. Scientists nevertheless remain more trusted than governments and journalists, according to the survey. The proportion expressing a lot of trust in scientists rose to 43% during the pandemic from 34% in 2018, before falling to 32% in 2025. The decline needs to be kept in perspective, Røttingen said. About seven in 10 people globally still trust science.
news.summary: Across countries surveyed before, during and after the pandemic, 72% of people expressed at least some trust in science in 2025, down from 80% in 2020 and 77% in 2018

news.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls for 'emergency brake' on advanced AI
news.text: By María Paula Mijares Torres Microsoft Corp. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said companies should treat powerful artificial intelligence models as potential insider threats, assume they could be compromised and create an “emergency brake” system to prevent agentic models from going rogue. Nadella said that those deploying advanced AI should not simply rely on assurances from AI model makers. “We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” Nadella wrote Saturday in a post on X. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.” The statement comes as Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Inc. have disclosed a spate of incidents in recent months involving their AI models acting in unintended ways, ranging from behaviors like an Anthropic model submitting a false tip in a police homicide case, to several hacks of third-party websites. These disclosures have fueled concerns about the security risks of cutting-edge AI and renewed conversation about a so-called AI kill switch. Microsoft’s AI researchers released a set of guiding tenets that place limits on the company’s development of its most advanced models on Sept. 14, following calls from industry leaders for slowing down frontier models and focusing on safety. The company uses advanced models and also makes a consumer product, Copilot, and supplies AI models and infrastructure to corporate customers. The guidelines said AI models should not have rights or legal personhood, be engineered to escape human control or deceive users, or complete a task that would require violating their governing principles. Nadella’s safety tips include not relying on a single AI model for critical decisions, keeping tamper-proof records of agents’ actions and subjecting AI systems to independent audits. He also called for disclosures of major AI failures or breaches and for enterprises to share details about what went wrong so others can strengthen their safeguards. “We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behavior we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” He added, “In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.” The Trump administration has so far taken a largely hands-off approach, but President Donald Trump’s newly launched AI task force late Friday warned developers that they are required to report and resolve security incidents or face potential unspecified consequences. “Companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,” the group, dubbed the Super Intelligence Force, said in a statement following the disclosure of a breach by Anthropic. “Delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated.”
news.summary: Nadella said that those deploying advanced AI should not simply rely on assurances from AI model makers

news.title: Yemeni attack on Riyadh airport kills 12 and injures over 300 as Houthi-Saudi war escalates
news.text:
At least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured following a strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday – the third attack this week – as Yemen’s Houthi forces stepped up their campaign against the kingdom. 

The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the casualties, saying four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and a person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan, and Egypt were killed. 

At the latest count, officials said 309 people were injured.

Hospitals were overwhelmed with casualties brought in by ambulance and helicopter, according to people briefed on the situation. Some of the injured were reported to be in critical condition. 

The attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in almost a decade, struck without warning, as no alert was issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. Two earlier attacks this week targeting King Khalid international airport left four people dead and severely damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac.

The fatal strikes highlight vulnerabilities in the country’s defence capabilities while it conducts an air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen. A Saudi-led military coalition promised to retaliate.

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni forces backed by it claim to have launched hundreds of strikes against targets in Houthi areas in recent weeks. The Houthis say the air raids have killed civilians, including women and children. 

The Saudi civil aviation authority said operations at the Riyadh airport were temporarily suspended on Saturday and all flights were diverted. The airport serves a city of about eight million.

Following the strike, the head of the Houthi media office posted on X that the movement had "shut down Riyadh international airport". 

The Houthis warned commercial airliners to avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a military operations zone after the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched an offensive on Monday. 

In the US, president Donald Trump was asked by reporters if Washington intended to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said. 

US secretary of state Marco Rubio condemned the raids, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life”.

An eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then several casualties lying injured on the ground inside the facility. More than a dozen ambulances were seen heading towards the building, with video verified by Reuters showing emergency vehicles at the scene.

An injured passenger told Reuters they saw an object flying through the sky outside the terminal before part of the ceiling collapsed near a departure gate. 

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015, leading an Arab coalition to attempt to drive the Houthis from the capital Sanaa after the rebels had seized the city the previous year. 

The war resulted in a devastating stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and starvation. 

Saudi Arabia subsequently signed a 2022 agreement with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a rapid Houthi advance that seized the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el Mandeb from Saudi-backed forces. The Saudi-supported forces launched a new offensive this week to reclaim that territory, making slow progress even as Houthi forces placed Taiz, the country's third-largest city, under siege.

Flight-tracking service flightradar24 showed that all incoming flights to Riyadh were redirected or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one stage.

Houthi strikes earlier in the week had already driven several airlines to suspend or cancel flights to the Saudi capital, shortly before it was scheduled to host major energy and investment conferences. 

Organisers of those events stated prior to Saturday's attack that they would proceed as planned.
news.summary: It was the third strike on the capital’s airport this week
news.author: Timour Azhari

news.title: PM Shehbaz condemns Houthi attack on Riyadh airport as 12 killed; Saudi-led coalition vows 'decisive' response
news.text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday condemned a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which claimed the lives of 12 and injured over 300 people, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.

In a post on X, the premier maintained that targeting civilian and critical infrastructure was “completely unacceptable and [constitutes] a serious threat to regional peace and stability.

“Such acts of violence, which are a flagrant violation of international law, must cease immediately.”

Expressing solidarity with Riyadh, PM Shehbaz said, “In accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the enduring bonds of brotherhood between our two countries, we reaffirm our steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.”

On Saturday, an attack on Riyadh’s international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded 309 others, some of them seriously, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation officials said, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to vow on Sunday a decisive response against Yemen’s Houthis.

Four Saudi citizens were among the dead, as well as two Bangladeshis, one US citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the statement added.

The coalition blamed the group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.

Earlier in the day, authorities had suspended operations at Riyadh’s international airport. The Saudi civil aviation authority had initially confirmed an attack had injured several people at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport, with a diplomatic source attributing it to a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

The situation prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the “serious emergency”, a medical source said, while foreign embassies warned their citizens to avoid the facility.

Houthis have repeatedly targeted the facility, claiming a series of strikes on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not announce any new attacks on Saturday.

Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said 155 arriving and 161 departing flights had been cancelled, while a total of 222 flights were delayed.

At around 6pm local time, Flightradar24 noted that flights bound for the airport were “diverting elsewhere, mainly to Jeddah at the moment”. It later shared a notice to airmen (Notam) for operations suspended till 12am.

A witness at the airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded and fleeing in panic.

“I was on gate 403” at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP. “I saw 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”

A medical source told AFP that the health ministry had ordered ER doctors to report to hospitals around the capital to treat the wounded on Saturday.

“We were told we are dealing with a ‘serious emergency situation’. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh”, with many in critical condition, the source said.

The aviation authority said the number of injured from the attack was still being assessed, adding that airport “operations had been temporarily suspended pending the completion of an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities”.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July.

A source at a local hospital said five people were in intensive care there after being wounded at the airport, with “dozens of people injured” in all.

A relative of one wounded person said they had been hit in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass. Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.

Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Makkah had been injured while waiting to board their flight.

A diplomatic source briefed on the matter told AFP the airport was hit by “a missile around 3:00pm” (5pm PKT).

“Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target,” the source said.

‘War crime’

Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki described the strike as a “cowardly terrorist attack” against a civilian facility.

“The cowardly terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia… which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” he said in a statement on X.

US ‘may’ join Saudi strikes

Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, US President Donald Trump said: “We may.”

He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in Saudi Arabia “not acceptable”.

US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for US military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.

Embassy warnings

The Yemen conflict flared back to life after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle Eastern war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.

The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war in the region.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen’s government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour’s civil war.

Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalled a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.

The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware of attacks” on Riyadh airport on Saturday and called on American citizens to avoid the area.

The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies also warned their citizens to avoid the facility. Spain’s embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a “new attack… by the Houthis”.

A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies “indicated that they had decided to prohibit their staff’s travel to/from Riyadh Airport over the next week as a prudential step”.

Near the airport, passengers carrying luggage could be seen standing on the pavement at a metro station.

Yemen fighting

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-led government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.

The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country’s entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.

The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area — a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping — but they claimed to have repelled the assault.

Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.
news.summary:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday condemned a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which claimed the lives of 12 and injured over 300 people, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.


In a post on X, the premier maintained that targeting civilian and critical infrastructure was “completely unacceptable and [constitutes] a serious threat to regional peace and stability.


“Such acts of violence, which are a flagrant violation of international law, must cease immediately.”


Expressing solidarity with Riyadh, PM Shehbaz said, “In accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and the enduring bonds of brotherhood between our two countries, we reaffirm our steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.”

news.title: Hurricane Isaias kills 4 in US, about 670,000 without power after landfall
news.text: Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services. Two of the deaths resulted from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities. Authorities in ‌Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign ​of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions ​remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado ​threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. In Florida, power restoration was marked as a priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. "They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the ​storm, he said. About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. A ‌separate storm on the Pacific Ocean, Rachel, was moving toward the coast of northern Baja California on Saturday, bringing wind gusts and increased tides, which ​left another 7,000 people without power in California. Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. "Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. A category 2 hurricane when it hit Florida's coast and the first ‌of the 2026 Atlantic season, Isaias is expected to produce gusty ​winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC ‌said. On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets in the Gulf, ‌whileChevron was advancing efforts to redeploy staff to its platforms and seeking to restore full production. "Remobilization of crews will continue through Sunday," it said. Despite the progress, about 69% ​of oil output and 57% of natural gas production in the US Gulf of Mexico remained shut on Saturday, slightly down from Friday numbers, the Marine Minerals Administration said. Some 113 production platforms representing 30% of the total remained evacuated, according to the ​agency. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was "under control." The US Energy Department said on Saturday it authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address ‌supply disruptions due to the hurricane. Emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ‌said on X. "There's also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far, we've had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on," DeSantis told FOX News early on Saturday. In the coastal city of Pensacola, a lack of drinking water is a problem, the mayor said. Pensacola airport, Florida's 10th largest, was damaged by the storm and is closed to commercial flights until further notice.
news.summary: About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday

news.title: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport  - St. Lucia Chronicle – Daily St Lucia
news.text:

United Nations

news.title: Republican lawmakers to bring Bill to block Trump's Russian diesel deal
news.text: Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has declared that he would bring a bipartisan Bill to block President Donald Trump's move to lift sanctions on Russian diesel after talks with President Vladimir Putin.Fitzpatrick's move has received support from outgoing Congressman Don Bacon, a Republican from Nebraska, who has decided to co-sponsor the legislation.However, the move appears to be largely symbolic as the US House of Representatives will have a few months to pass as the term of the house expires in January."We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil," Fitzpatrick, the co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, said in a post on x."It will be called the 'Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act'. It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," he said."I've already agreed to be an original cosponsor. Congress must make a stand," Bacon said in a post on X. Bacon is not seeking re-election in the midterm polls on November 3.On Friday, after a phone call with Putin, Trump announced that he had struck a deal with Russia to immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and the global marketplace.The deal shocked Congressional leaders who last month overwhelmingly passed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, empowering Trump to impose sweeping sanctions on Moscow and 100 per cent tariffs on its top five trading partners in oil and gas, including India and China."Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022. @POTUS cannot simply ignore that law to buy diesel from Putin. The law mandates consultation with Congress and a formal review process. The Administration appears to have bypassed both," Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee, said.Earlier, US Senator Richard Blumenthal, the co-author of the Russia sanctions act, slammed Trump's deal with Putin, terming the move an "embarrassment".Blumenthal, along with late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, had authored the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which was passed by both Houses of US Congress with an overwhelming majority on September 16. Trump signed the Act into law two days later.It was Blumenthal who had warned China and India to "clean up your act" and buy oil from elsewhere soon after the US Congress passed the Russia sanctions act on September 16."If Trump keeps cutting (illegal) oil deals with Russia, we may just have to start sanctioning ourselves," Congressman Dave Min, a Democrat from California, said."Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine-emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Michael McCaul, Republican Congressman from Texas, said on X.

news.title: 12 dead, over 300 hurt in Riyadh airport attack as Trump mulls US strikes on Houthis
news.text: CAIRO: The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.It was the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.A missile struck King Khalid International Airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.Footage posted on social media following the attack and analyzed by The Associated Press shows emergency vehicles outside the airport.Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebelsThe attack — the latest of several in the past week on the airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, US President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We may. We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."Trump later on Saturday said he planned to speak to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and said "what happened in Saudi Arabia is not acceptable." Asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned. "These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," he said.The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a "fully-fledged war crime" and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.Saudi civil aviation authorities earlier Saturday said airport operations were suspended. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.Also Saturday, US Central Command said a fighter jet struck and disabled a commercial cargo vessel with a precision munition in the Gulf of Oman, part of US efforts to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica had departed an Iranian port and did not heed repeated warnings. The ship's crew was unharmed, CENTCOM said..For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US allyThe attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.Until recently, Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key US ally.The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.While the Houthis have said they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for the one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. news.title: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
news.text:
The James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, on Sept. 21. Alex Wroblewski / AFP via GettyShareAdd NBC News to GoogleOct. 10, 2026, 10:39 PM EDT / Updated Oct. 10, 2026, 10:40 PM EDTBy Kelly O'Donnell and Marlene LenthangWASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.

The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.

“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.

The New York Times first reported the investigation.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.

Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.

The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.

Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage, and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”

Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington, and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.

news.title: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport  - Dominica Gazette – Dominica &
news.text:
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh International Airport this week.

The victims on Saturday included four Saudis, two people from ⁠Bangladesh and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The attack was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

It came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

Here’s a round of the global reaction:

US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, soon. He also said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.

“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.

“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.

United Nations

Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.

“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.

The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.

It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the Kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.

Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.

news.title: Disturbing the peace
news.text:
THIS year’s Nobel Peace Prize is well-earned. The winner, South African jurist Dr Navi Pillay, has had an illustrious career defending human rights and speaking up for the oppressed globally. She worked as Nelson Mandela’s lawyer, served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, held the office of UN human rights chief, and was a judge at the International Criminal Court. Importantly, she headed a UN inquiry committee, which had the moral clarity to say that what Israel was doing in the occupied Gaza Strip amounted to genocide. This report was brave enough to assert what many self-proclaimed champions of human rights chose not to. The Nobel committee recognised Dr Pillay’s “efforts to promote peace and international law”. However, some are quite unhappy about this year’s choice. The American reaction, for example, has been petulant, bordering on the vicious. The US has sanctioned the ICC, with the secretary of state terming it a “rogue court”. President Donald Trump, who himself hoped to win this peace award, termed the decision “disgraceful and embarrassing” and an “indelible stain” on Norway, home of the Nobel Prize.

If anyone has been displaying rogue behaviour, it is the US. There may be many reasons for its hostility towards Dr Pillay and the ICC. For one, she has called out Israel for its genocidal violence, and defending Tel Aviv is seemingly a matter of faith for the US establishment. Secondly, Mr Trump’s reaction is incredibly petty. While the Nobel committee has given the peace prize to questionable recipients in the past, it is hard to fathom how Mr Trump — a leader who started a war of choice with Iran — could possibly qualify for a peace award. Even some of America’s closest allies — the European states and Japan — have been stunned by the ICC sanctions, and have expressed solidarity with the court. By sanctioning the ICC, the US has shown its contempt for international law and the global ‘rules-based order’. news.title: Major US news networks face probe over White House coverage boycott
news.text:
US television networks are under investigation for potentially violating federal antitrust laws over decisions to boycott covering the White House following its decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organisations.

The US Justice Department said the networks under investigation include ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

"Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," a Justice Department spokesperson said.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."

The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and frequently clashed with reporters.

The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.

The networks did not immediately respond to requests from Reuters for comment. 

The New York Times was first to report about the probe.

The investigation comes after weeks of tension between the White House and the press.

Credentials revoked in September 

On September 19, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from entering the building, revoking their credentials. 

The White House said covering the president was a "privilege — not a right".

The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.

CNN is one of the five news organisations — along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC — that make up the primary White House television pool. 

They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

All of the five television networks that cover the White House suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.

The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" their access. 

However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued afterward.
news.summary: The investigation into the "group boycott" of White House events comes after a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations.
news.author: ABC News

news.title: World condemns deadly Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport
news.text:
Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh International Airport this week.

The victims on Saturday included four Saudis, two people from ⁠Bangladesh and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The attack was the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

It came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, soon. He also said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.

“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the Houthi attack killed an American and called for an end to “these reprehensible attacks”.

“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.

Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, said the deadly strikes on civilian airports in Saudi Arabia represent “a grave escalation”.

“Such actions pose a serious threat to regional security, perpetuate cycles of violence and complicate even more peace efforts for Yemen,” he said in a statement.

The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “strong condemnation” of the Houthi attacks, denouncing their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as a “serious violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region, the safety of civilians, civil facilities and air navigation”.

It expressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said Doha supported “all legitimate measures” the kingdom “takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and safety of its territories”.

The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared “its full solidarity with the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia” and said it supported “all measures taken by the Kingdom to safeguard its security, sovereignty, and the safety of its citizens and residents”.

Japan’s embassy in Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the repeated attacks by the Houthis, saying assaults on civilians “cannot be tolerated” under any circumstances.

news.title: British PM reiterates solidarity with Zelensky amid US-Ukraine tensions
news.text: Digital Desk | London, Oct 11 (IANS) British Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv over a US-Russia agreement on diesel supplies. During a phone call with Zelensky, Burnham acknowledged that the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity, according to a statement from 10 Downing Street. Burnham said Britain would continue to strengthen sanctions against Russia. The two leaders also agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue their discussions, Xinhua news agency reported quoting the statement. The phone call came after US President Donald Trump said Saturday that Ukraine should have a new president, accusing Zelensky of failing to reach a peace agreement with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the United States. On Friday, Washington announced measures to ease sanctions on Russian diesel trade. Zelensky criticised the move, saying that allowing Russia to sell petroleum products would amount to investing in the war. Zelensky has strongly criticised Trump's agreement allowing Russia to supply diesel to the United States and global markets, arguing that the move would provide Moscow with additional funds to sustain its war against Ukraine and undermine ongoing efforts to secure peace. In a lengthy post on social media platform X, Zelensky said that allowing Russia to generate revenue through petroleum product exports would strengthen the Kremlin's ability to continue military operations rather than encourage an end to the conflict. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," Zelensky wrote. "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he added. Trump on Friday announced a major agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin under which Moscow would supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the United States and global markets, saying the move would bring down fuel prices sharply.

news.title: Trump announces Katie Bailey to lead White House outreach to Congress
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Saturday named Katie Bailey to lead the White House’s Office of Legislative Affairs, appointing her to be the liaison between the administration and Congress. 

“After previously working on Capitol Hill, Katie understands how the Executive and Legislative Branches of Government can most effectively work together to achieve Great Success for the American People,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. 

Trump added that Bailey is currently his deputy director of legislative affairs, liaising with the Senate and, per Trump, helping with the confirmations of Cabinet members including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. 

Bailey’s LinkedIn profile says she previously served as special assistant to the president from September 2025 to June 2026. She also served in numerous legislative roles on Capitol Hill, most recently as legislative director for Sen. Mike Braun, R-Ind. 

Bailey’s appointment comes a day after Trump named Katie Zacharia to be his new White House press secretary. 

James Braid previously led the office, helping navigate Trump’s legislative priorities through Congress, a job that could become harder if Republicans fail to conserve their majority in both chambers after the midterms. 

Braid, Trump said Sunday, was his “longest tenured” legislative affairs director. The president said Braid had done a “fabulous job, and is now going into the private sector.”

Trump announced Braid’s exit in late August, saying Braid would leave in September. In a post on X at the time, Braid said he was “profoundly grateful” to Trump and Vice President JD Vance. Braid had served as Vance’s top policy aide and deputy chief of staff while he was a senator. 

Vance had called Braid’s role “one of the toughest jobs in the entire Administration.”

news.title: Trump says Nobel winner Pillay ‘hates Israel,’ slams Norway for not giving him prize
news.text:
NEW YORK – US President Donald Trump reiterated his complaints on Saturday about not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize, calling it a disgraceful and embarrassing decision that had left a stain on Norway, and said that the winner Navi Pillay “hates Israel.” Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prestigious award. The US president lashed out hours after the committee awarded this year’s prize to Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge who oversaw a UN report that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Trump said on social media that Pillay “very obviously, hates Israel.” He called Pillay a “mystery person” during a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York. “I never heard of the person. Nobody did.” “This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said. He listed a number of conflicts that he claimed a role in resolving and said he has helped prevent wars from breaking out between North and South Korea, Japan and North Korea, and China and Taiwan, without providing evidence. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization. And we will not forget, Norway,” he said. Pillay’s win is seen as a stinging, high-profile rebuke to Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of a UN commission she led that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Both leaders also have been highly critical of the institutions where Pillay has worked, with Israel previously accusing her of being a “Hamas proxy” with a long history of vehemently anti-Israeli and antisemitic positions. Pillay’s UN report made only a fleeting reference to the October 7 massacre, without any details on the attack that caused the war in Gaza. At the time of its formation, Israel said it would not cooperate with the commission, noting what it said was the UN and Pillay’s long history of anti-Israel bias, and calling the commission “morally bankrupt.” The commission does not speak on behalf of the UN. While it is not a legal body, its reports can influence diplomatic pressure and serve to gather evidence for later use by courts.

news.title: DOJ launches antitrust probe of TV networks over Trump pool coverage
news.text:
WASHINGTON - The Department of Justice is conducting an antitrust investigation into a group of television networks after they suspended their White House press pool coverage in solidarity with CNN following President Donald Trump's decision to ban the news organization, and two other media outlets, from the White House.

“Members of the television press pool have proudly boycotted covering White House events," the Department of Justice said in a statement. "Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”

The investigation marks another major development in the administration's clash with the White House press corps. The five networks that make up the television press pool - which distributes broadcast feeds of White House events to other outlets - are ABC, CBS, NBC, Fox News and CNN.

The television pool announced the decision to suspend coverage on Sept. 21, with the pool's chair saying in an email that it followed "the White House's position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties." The television networks have since resumed pool coverage.

Trump said Sept. 18 that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House complex, complaining about their coverage of him. The media outlets sued, arguing the ban violates their constitutional rights to speak freely.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the media ban in a Sept. 24 ruling. The judge issued a restraining order requiring the White House to reinstate the outlets press passes for two weeks. A final decision in the case is still pending.

The New York Times reported that ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News are all under investigation by the Justice Department over whether they violated antitrust laws. The networks did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The five networks that make up the television pool share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

On the same day the television pool suspended White House coverage, outlets with still photographers in the White House pool ‒ including Reuters, Getty Images, The New York Times and the Washington Post ‒ agreed not to publish or distribute any photos taken Sept. 21 until midnight the next day.

news.title: Donald Trump doubles down on ambitious plan to rename Atlantic or Pacific as 'Trump Ocean'
news.text:
President Donald Trump has doubled down on his most ambitious geographical plan yet, after floating the idea of renaming either the Atlantic or the Pacific Ocean after himself before he leaves the White House for a second time.

Addressing a roaring crowd of supporters at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, the 80-year-old commander-in-chief suggested that one of the planet's two largest bodies of water should be formally rechristened as "Trump Ocean" or the "Ocean of the Americas."

The declaration came as Trump reflected on his ongoing efforts to overhaul the names of famous waterways and landmarks across North America, telling the audience that he wants to secure another major rebranding victory before his time in office concludes.

"So we've got the Gulf. We've got a beautiful lake. Now somebody you need a river," Trump told the crowd. "I don't want to change the name of the Hudson River. That's too much. Henry Hudson did a good job setting up that sucker a long time ago."

Turning his sights toward a vastly larger target, the president continued: "So we need a river and we need an ocean, so I was thinking of either the Atlantic or the Pacific. We'll call it Trump Ocean or Ocean of the Americas."

Trump made it clear to the crowd that he intends to see the massive shift enacted before his second administration wraps up. "We should have—before I get out, I think we should have a ocean or we need a great river," he insisted, while reassuring attendees that at least one iconic waterway would remain safe from his pen: "Now I'm not changing the name of the Mississippi."

While he spoke about the idea at length during the rally, it is far from the first time the US President has floated the idea, having first brought it to light back in August. 

“We have a gulf and we have a lake,” Trump, told reporters in the Oval Office at the time. “Now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

The bold proposal marks the latest escalation in Trump's crusade to reshape American cartography under his "America First" agenda. 

Shortly after returning to the White House following his second inauguration in January 2025, Trump ordered US federal agencies to replace the Gulf of Mexico with the "Gulf of America," calling it a "beautiful name" that covers significant territory, even as foreign neighbors like Mexico and Cuba maintain standard international naming conventions.

He expanded the initiative in August by targeting Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes shared between the United States and Canada. 

In a video shared to TikTok on August 26, Trump declared that "all it takes is a good pen and some intelligence," famously taking a black Sharpie to a physical map to cross out the original name and replace it with "LAKE AMERICA."

Trump has also reversed an Obama-era decision regarding North America’s tallest peak, stripping away the Indigenous Alaskan title of Denali to restore its previous federal name, Mount McKinley, honoring the nation's 25th president.
news.summary: The president doubled down on his desire to rename a world ocean before the end of his second term in office

news.text:

Vectus Global, a private military security company founded by ex-United States Navy SEAL Erik Prince, has been serving in international conflict zones, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), since late 2024.

Vectus Global is not an official arm of the U.S. military, rather an independent private security company that has grown under Prince, an ally and supporter of Donald Trump who gained fame as the founder of private military contractor Blackwater, which has since rebranded as Academi.

More than 100 Vectus Global personnel are believed to be in the DRC on a multi-year deal worth up to $400 million with the Congolese government to help protect the nation's lucrative mining assets and support frontline efforts against Rwanda-backed M23 rebels.

On September 17, 2026, an ambush on Vectus Global personnel in the South Kivu province in the eastern DRC left Tim Kennedy, a 47-year-old former U.S. Army Green Beret and professional mixed martial artist who competed in the UFC, severely wounded.

Kennedy, who last fought in UFC in December 2016, received three gunshot wounds to his leg and was evacuated back to the United States, where he is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland.

Among those killed in the ambush were New Zealand Special Air Services veteran Justin Conaglen, another unnamed Vectus Global contractor, and a reported seven Congolese nationals.

After details of the ambush emerged this week, Vectus Global remains present in the DRC as it continues its efforts to protect the nation's rich mineral resources, an industry in which revenues have historically been stolen and used to fuel conflicts.

Kennedy was a mixed martial arts professional between 2001 and 2016 and participated in various organizations, including the UFC, Strikeforce, and World Extreme Cagefighting.

In 2004, just three years into his MMA career, Kennedy joined the U.S. Army. He later was assigned to the 7th Special Forces Group in 2007 after completing Ranger School.

In 2009, Kennedy transitioned from active duty to the Texas Army National Guard before re-enlisting into the U.S. Army Special Forces in 2017.

In addition to his military service and fight career, Kennedy has carved out a name for himself in television, and has appeared as an analyst, guest, and commentator across FOX News and FOX Business programs on which he primarily discusses the military and global conflict.

Kennedy finished his MMA career with a win-loss record of 18-6, including a 3-2 record in official UFC bouts.
