news.title: What Is the Sherman Act? Why DOJ Investigating Networks Over Trump Coverage
news.text: The Justice Department is investigating whether five major television networks violated federal antitrust law when they briefly suspended pooled coverage of President Donald Trump after CNN was barred from White House grounds. ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and Fox News were contacted by Justice Department officials on Friday and asked to provide communications and other materials related to the White House television pool, The New York Times first reported. The pool is a longstanding arrangement under which participating networks share responsibility for covering the president and distributing footage to other outlets. The inquiry stems from the networks' decision last month to halt pooled coverage for several days after the Trump administration barred CNN journalists from the White House, preventing the network from participating in the pool. The networks later coverage after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order on September 24 requiring the White House to restore access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The Justice Department publicly acknowledged the Sherman Act inquiry on Saturday. "Members of the television press pool have proudly boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," a Justice Department spokesperson told Newsweek. Newsweek has also reached out to ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News for comment. What is the Sherman Act? The Sherman Antitrust Act, signed into law in 1890, is one of the cornerstone laws governing competition in the United States. The statute broadly prohibits agreements that restrain trade and bars efforts to monopolize markets. According to Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, the law outlaws contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrict interstate commerce and prohibits monopolization or attempts to monopolize a market. The act's two principal sections address different forms of anticompetitive conduct. Section 1 targets agreements among competitors that restrain trade, while Section 2 prohibits monopolization and attempts to monopolize. Violations can lead to civil enforcement actions and, in some circumstances, criminal prosecution by the Justice Department. The Sherman Act has been used in some of the country's most significant antitrust cases. It played a role in the breakup of Standard Oil in 1911 and AT&T in 1984, and has more recently been central to major government cases involving Microsoft and Google. Why is DOJ Citing the Sherman Act? The investigation appears to focus on whether the networks' coordinated decision to suspend pooled coverage could amount to what antitrust law describes as a group boycott. The Justice Department is examining whether the networks acted collectively when they stopped providing pool footage after CNN's exclusion from the White House, The New York Times reported. The department's public comments have focused on alleged coordination among competing media organizations. The television pool consists of CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. Reuters reported that the organizations share coverage costs, rotate responsibility for gathering footage, and distribute video to news outlets across the country. The dispute began after Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House on September 18, citing what he described as "purposely negative stories," according to The New York Times. The three organizations sued, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights. A federal judge later temporarily blocked the restrictions, with that order scheduled to expire Tuesday. The legal and political standoff between the Trump administration and the White House press corps escalated Monday after Politico was blocked from traveling aboard Air Force One. The move prevented the news organization from carrying out its scheduled duties as the designated print representative in the presidential travel pool, adding a new front to an increasingly contentious dispute over press access. "We can confirm that Politico was excluded from today’s out-of-town travel pool," a Politico spokesperson told Newsweek. "We do not have additional comment at this time, but would refer you back to our legal filings, previous statements and those from our attorney, Ted Boutrous." The White House declined to comment when reached by Newsweek about the Politico Air Force One ban. A New Front in Trump's Media Battles The reported investigation marks the latest clash between the Trump administration and major news organizations. The Justice Department has previously subpoenaed reporters from the New York Times and seized a laptop belonging to a Washington Post journalist. The Associated Press has waged a separate legal battle with the Trump administration over White House access since February 2025, when the administration restricted its journalists from some presidential events after the outlet continued using the name “Gulf of Mexico” instead of Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America.” The AP sued, alleging retaliation for its editorial decisions and a violation of the First Amendment. A federal judge initially ordered the White House to restore access, but an appeals court later allowed the restrictions to remain while the case proceeded. Reuters and HuffPost have not faced the same broader restrictions, but reporters from both outlets were excluded from Trump’s first Cabinet meeting in February 2025. Reuters had long participated in the presidential press pool, while HuffPost was scheduled to provide that day’s print pool reporter before being replaced. Whether the DOJ's Sherman Act investigation ultimately results in any enforcement action remains unclear. For now, the Justice Department has said it is examining whether the networks' actions violated federal antitrust laws. news.summary: DOJ is investigating whether major TV networks violated antitrust law by suspending White House pool coverage.

news.title: Trump’s trade wars sting US manufacturers ahead of midterms
news.text:
Published: 21:33 EDT, 10 October 2026 | Updated: 21:33 EDT, 10 October 2026

Building materials at Shapes Unlimited, a US manufacturer in North Jackson, Ohio facing millions of dollars in additional costs due to President Donald Trump’s aluminum tariffs

For Doug Rende, who runs an aluminum product manufacturer in the US state of Ohio, President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant millions of dollars more in annual costs — and recently, the Iran war has made shipments even more expensive.

Rende is chief executive at Shapes Unlimited, one of many American producers smarting from Trump’s economic policies as midterm elections approach.

“Frustrating would be one word,” Rende told AFP.

“And I think that we’re sensing a lack of trust in not only the administration but the governmental process, the role of Congress to rein in executive power,” he added.

Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products and countries.

Besides aluminum, the duties hit steel and autos too, while US trading partners face additional tariffs that vary by country.

Even as some American manufacturers have benefited as their foreign competitors encounter higher barriers, others struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty.

Trump’s spiraling trade fight with Canada and war with Iran have only deepened worries.

Grievances over Trump’s trade policies are among fault lines that Democrats hope will work in their favor as they push to flip control of the Senate and House of Representatives in November’s vote.

Shapes Unlimited CEO Doug Rende at his company’s warehouse

Rende’s company in North Jackson, Ohio, makes and distributes aluminum building products used in fixtures like fences.

Trump’s tariffs on aluminum have steadily climbed, from 10 percent during his first presidency to 25 percent and then 50 percent last year, and Rende has felt the impact.

“This year alone, it’s upwards of $4.5 million to $5 million in additional costs,” Rende said.

“There’s only so much that the end consumer is willing to eat,” he added. “So, we absorb a healthy portion.”

These added costs include steeper transportation fees, as fuel prices surged with the US-Israel war on Iran. Surcharges are “upwards of $6,500 per container” of goods from suppliers, Rende said.

As a result, he has paused recruitment for new jobs while investing in more robotic assembly.

Sam Miller, another Ohio manufacturer who makes kitchen and bathroom products, has been hit on both fronts in Trump’s trade wars, paying tariffs on imported materials from Asia while finding it harder to expand into Canada because of trade tensions.

“It’s been difficult for businesses to manage,” Miller told AFP from his factory floor in Warren as a machine hummed nearby, cutting countertop material. “I do think that there will be a shift away from Republican views.”

Although Miller received refunds after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s duties, the US leader has since reinstated many of them.

A worker at Sam Miller’s factory, which produces kitchen and bathroom products, in Warren, Ohio,

Deteriorating US-Canada ties add to his challenges, with Washington and Ottawa slapping tariffs on each other’s products after trade negotiations collapsed in August.

“We’re selling into Canada and it is particularly straining on both us and our customers,” Miller said.

He originally planned on opening a distribution facility in Canada this year, but progress has slowed.

Guy Coviello, president of the Youngstown Warren Regional Chamber, told AFP he is monitoring tariffs, the Iran war and immigration very closely.

These are a “mixed bag” for firms but negative overall, said Coviello, whose business group has some 3,000 members.

Some firms have lost customers or had to downsize, he said.

Canada is also Ohio’s biggest export market, with a third of Ohio’s exports going to the country.

“Where it gets even more complicated is that there are some goods that go back and forth across the border multiple times,” he said.

The Iran war adds to stresses, raising freight costs and hitting aluminum supplies due to drone attacks in the Middle East.

With a lack of new US aluminum smelters, Coviello said: “We are all for tariffs for critical items such as defense and medical industry.”

But he added: “We have to be careful when you’re talking about products that are not crucial and are not available in the US.”
